title: Engineering logical gates with irrep surface codes
authors: Yabo Li, Zijian Song, Vieri Mattei, Naren Manjunath, Apoorv Tiwari, Tyler D. Ellison
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation typically relies on a fixed set of logical primitives, while realizing other desired operations can require substantial resources. We introduce irrep surface codes (ISCs), two-dimensional topological quantum error-correcting codes engineered to transversally implement a prescribed set of logical gates. The engineered gates only need to satisfy two conditions: (i) they generate a finite group, which, up to global phases, is forced by the Eastin-Knill theorem, and (ii) they are irreducible, meaning that any operator commuting with the set of gates must be proportional to the identity. This accommodates arbitrary finite groups of diagonal gates and arbitrary reversible classical gates, since each can be embedded into a larger irreducible finite group of gates. It also enables logical gates outside every finite level of the Clifford hierarchy. To incorporate these operations into surface-code computations, we further develop lattice-surgery protocols to transfer the encoded information between surface codes and ISCs obeying either of two sufficient conditions. Together, these results establish a systematic method for tailoring topological codes to desired logical operations and integrating them into conventional computations.
summary: This paper introduces Irrep Surface Codes (ISCs), a novel class of topological quantum error-correcting codes designed to implement arbitrary, desired logical gates. By constructing these codes based on the projective representations of a target gate group, the authors establish a systematic method for tailoring topological codes. Furthermore, they provide protocols to integrate these specialized ISCs into existing surface-code computations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a systematic method to engineer topological quantum error-correcting codes that can transversally implement arbitrary desired logical gates, especially those outside the standard Clifford hierarchy.
main_result: They introduce Irrep Surface Codes (ISCs) that can be constructed to implement any gate set $G$ derived from an irreducible finite group, and they provide lattice-surgery protocols to integrate these ISCs with standard surface codes.
method: The core method involves constructing the ISC based on the projective irreducible representation ($\Gamma$) of the target gate group $G$, and developing lattice-surgery protocols for code state transfer.
model_or_system: The physical model is the Irrep Surface Code (ISC), a 2D topological quantum error-correcting code defined on a triangular patch with specific boundary conditions. The gates are engineered to realize an arbitrary irreducible finite group $G$.
key_observables: The implemented logical gates, the size of the gate group $|G|$, and the dimension of the projective irrep $\Gamma$.
important_parameters: The structure of the finite group $G$ (e.g., its irreducibility and its relationship to Pauli operators) and the lattice geometry.
main_assumptions: The transfer protocols require the group $G$ to satisfy specific structural conditions, such as containing generalized Pauli X and Z operators or being generated by diagonal gates and Pauli X operators.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the process of building an ISC from an irreducible finite group $G$ via its projective irrep. Figure 2 shows the lattice structure of the ISC on a triangular patch with three boundary types.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework for engineering ISCs from an irreducible finite group $G$ using its projective irrep. It then details the construction of the ISC structure and concludes by developing lattice-surgery protocols to connect these specialized codes to conventional surface codes.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, systematic tool for designing quantum hardware primitives, moving beyond the limitations of standard gate sets by tailoring the code structure directly to the required computational logic.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: From G to an ISC. Starting with an irreducible finite group G, we define a projective irrep of the quotient group G. We then use the projective irrep of G to build an ISC. This ISC admits the gates of G as transversal logical operators, up to a global phase.

FIG. 2: Lattice for the ISC. The ISC is defined on a triangular patch with three different boundary conditions: rough, smooth, and twisted. These are distinguished by their associated stabilizers. The edges are assigned an orientation, which is used in the definition of the stabilizers.

FIG. 3: Mapping a flux-free state to the corner gauge. (a) Starting with an arbitrary flux-free state, we apply vertex stabilizers to map the leftmost edges to the identity. This produces group elements labeled with primes on the connected edges. (b) We apply vertex stabilizers on the next column of vertices to map the horizontal edges on their left to the identity element. (c) After removing the group elements from the horizontal edges, we apply the corner stabilizer. This enacts a representation operator on the Γ-corner. FIG. 4: For the rough-rough surgery, we merge an ISC and a surface code patch from the left, along with a column of ancillary qubits on the seam (denoted by the dashed red lines) by measuring the seam stabilizers. During this merging, a measurement of the joint logical operator (denoted by the thickened blue edges) is performed. The merged code can be split by making a Z measurement on each ancillary qubit on the seam, and local actions conditioned on the measurement outcomes.

FIG. 5: For the smooth-smooth surgery, we merge an ISC and a surface code patch from the bottom, along with a row of ancillary qubits on the seam (denoted by the dashed red lines) by measuring the seam stabilizers. During this merging, a measurement of the joint logical operator (denoted by the thickened blue edges) is performed. The merged code can be split by making an X measurement on each ancillary qubit on the seam, and local actions conditioned on the measurement outcomes.
